overview.text: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) is issuing the first federal fuel-economy rule for light trucks, vans, and jeep-type four-wheel-drive vehicles (called 'nonpassenger automobiles') rated at 6,000 pounds gross vehicle weight or less, for model year 1979 only. Manufacturers must achieve a production-weighted fleet average of 17.2 miles per gallon, or may elect a split standard of 17.2 mpg for other nonpassenger automobiles plus 15.8 mpg for jeep-type vehicles, with a $5 penalty per 0.1 mpg shortfall per vehicle. The rule directly affects domestic manufacturers — General Motors, Ford, Chrysler, American Motors, and International Harvester — plus captive imports (foreign-built pickups like the Chevrolet LUV and Ford Courier sold by domestic firms). NHTSA considered but rejected taking no action, extending the standard to trucks over 6,000 pounds (data not available), and setting higher or lower levels, ultimately lowering its proposed 18.7 mpg to 17.2 mpg to reflect an 8 percent fuel-economy loss from revised EPA test procedures. The primary environmental benefit is roughly 102.5 million gallons of gasoline saved annually (about 0.07-0.1 percent of 1975 U.S. consumption), with minor secondary effects from increased use of aluminum, plastics, and catalytic-converter metals. Every affected manufacturer objected that the proposed level was too high given 1979 emission and test-procedure changes, and no consumer or public-interest groups submitted substantive comments.

evidence.quote: This notice establishes average fuel economy standards for nonpassenger automobiles which are rated at 6,000 pounds gross vehicle weight or less and are manufactured in model year 1979.
The standard for four-wheel drive nonpassenger automobiles which are jeep-type vehicles is 15.8 mpg. The standard for all other nonpassenger automobiles is 17.2 mpg.

a manufacturer who fails to comply with an AFES will be liable for a civil penalty equal to $5 for each tenth of a mile per gallon by which the manufacturer's average fuel economy falls below the applicable AFES
Captive imports are vehicles, such as the Chevrolet LUV and the Ford Courier pickup trucks, which are marketed by a domestic manufacturer but fabricated by a foreign manufacturer.

The basic alternatives considered are: a. Take no action, b. Extend the scope of the standard to NPA's above 6,000 pounds GVWR, c. Make the standard effective for years beyond MY 1979, and d. Set a higher or lower standard.
Therefore, in the final rule, the proposed standard of 18.7 mpg is lowered to 17.2 mpg.
The agency estimates that 102,500,000 gallons of gasoline will be saved annually by the 1979 nonpassenger automobile fleet, over 1976 levels.
The annual and lifetime savings in gasoline would be between 0.07 percent and 0.1 percent of total national consumption based on total national consumption per year of 10.2 billion gallons in 1975.
Most of the comments were submitted by automobile manufacturers. There were no comments received from consumer groups, or other public interest organizations.

Virtually all manufacturers of nonpassenger automobiles who submitted comments indicated their belief that the level of the standard was too high, in light of the effects of emissions and other factors.

project_description.text: NHTSA is setting the first federal fuel-economy standard for model year 1979 'nonpassenger automobiles' — pickup trucks, vans, and jeep-type four-wheel-drive vehicles rated at 6,000 pounds gross vehicle weight or less — as required by section 502(b) of Title V of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act. The final rule sets 17.2 mpg for the general class and 15.8 mpg for jeep-type vehicles (four-wheel drive, off-highway capable, wheelbase not more than 110 inches), with manufacturers allowed to include their jeep-type vehicles in the general 17.2 mpg fleet at their option. Compliance is measured as a production-weighted average across each manufacturer's fleet, and the proposed level of 18.7 mpg was lowered by 8 percent to reflect measured effects of revised EPA test procedures.

evidence.quote: Vehicles affected by these standards include pickup trucks, vans, and four-wheel drive, jeep-type vehicles which are rated within that weight range.

section 502(b) of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act directs the Secretary of Transportation to prescribe automotive fuel economy standards for automobiles which are "not passenger automobiles" in model years which begin more than 30 months after the date of enactment of Title V.
The standard for four-wheel drive nonpassenger automobiles which are jeep-type vehicles is 15.8 mpg. The standard for all other nonpassenger automobiles is 17.2 mpg.
"Jeep-type vehicle" means a 4-wheel drive, general purpose automobile capable of off-highway operation that has a wheelbase not more than 110 inches
Each manufacturer of jeep-type vehicles will have the option of including those vehicles in the separate class, or including those vehicles in the general class of nonpassenger automobiles.
Title V requires that the production-weighted average fuel economy of all of a manufacturer's automobiles subject to the AFES equal or exceed the level of that AFES.
Therefore, in the final rule, the proposed standard of 18.7 mpg is lowered to 17.2 mpg.

affected_community.text: The rule directly affects U.S. light-truck manufacturers — General Motors, Ford, Chrysler, American Motors Corporation, and International Harvester — because domestic nonpassenger automobiles average much lower fuel economy than imports (15.9 mpg for all domestics compared with 22.1 mpg for imports in MY 1976). Total MY 1979 domestic production was projected at about 1 million vehicles (52.6% GM, 27.9% Ford, 16.3% Chrysler, 3.7% AMC), plus about 100,000 'captive imports' — foreign-built pickups such as the Chevrolet LUV (built by Isuzu) and Ford Courier (built by Toyo-Kogyo) sold by domestic firms. Consumers, the United Auto Workers, and the U.S. Forest Service also weighed in, the Forest Service concerned that design constraints would push truck buyers toward heavier, costlier vehicles.

evidence.quote: the development of the AFES concentrated on domestic NPA's since their fuel economy is considerably below that of imported NPA's (15.9 mpg for all domestics compared to 22.1 for all imports in MY 1976).
Total domestic production in MY 1979 was assumed to be 1 million vehicles of which 52.6 percent were GM, 27.9 percent were Ford, 16.3 percent were Chrysler, and 3.7 percent were AMC.
it was assumed that GM and Ford would each sell 50,000 captive imports in MY 1979.
Captive imports are vehicles, such as the Chevrolet LUV and the Ford Courier pickup trucks, which are marketed by a domestic manufacturer but fabricated by a foreign manufacturer.
The Forest Service expressed concern that fuel economy goals will force manufacturers to design tracks in a limited manner which inhibits their usefulness in a variety of applications.
Comments were received from General Motors, Ford, Chrysler, AMC and International Harvester.

alternatives_overview.text: NHTSA considered four principal alternatives: taking no action (rejected because the statute requires a standard); extending the standard to nonpassenger automobiles between 6,000 and 10,000 pounds gross vehicle weight (rejected because EPA baseline fuel-economy data for heavier trucks were not yet available); setting standards for model years beyond 1979 (deferred to future rulemakings because of uncertainty about market shifts to unregulated heavier vehicles); and setting a higher or lower level (a higher level was rejected because it could push consumers or manufacturers into the unregulated over-6,000-pound class, and a lower level was rejected as inconsistent with the Act's 'maximum feasible average fuel economy' requirement). The agency also considered whether to treat all nonpassenger automobiles as one class or split them, ultimately creating two classes with a separate 15.8 mpg level for jeep-type vehicles, and chose to include captive imports in domestic manufacturers' fleets for MY 1979 only.

evidence.quote: The basic alternatives considered are: a. Take no action, b. Extend the scope of the standard to NPA's above 6,000 pounds GVWR, c. Make the standard effective for years beyond MY 1979, and d. Set a higher or lower standard.

Section 502(b) of Title V of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act, 15 U.S.C. 2002(b), requires the Secretary of Transportation to prescribe, by rule, average fuel economy standards for nonpassenger automobiles (NPA's). Therefore this alternative was rejected.
Baseline fuel economy data from which to establish standards for MY 1979 were available from EPA for vehicles under 6,000 pounds GVWR. EPA could not supply data for heavier vehicles.
if either vehicles or consumer purchases are shifted to the over 6,000 pounds GVWR class, a reduction in fleet fuel economy could result
If the AFES is set at a lower level, the standard will not meet the requirement of "maximum feasible average fuel economy" established by the Act.

environmental_impact.text: The main environmental benefit is gasoline savings: about 102.5 million gallons annually versus 1976 levels (roughly 0.07-0.1 percent of the 10.2 billion gallons the U.S. consumed in 1975), or 691 million to 1.027 billion gallons over the fleet's 10-year lifetime, equivalent to 18.13 to 26.9 million barrels of oil. Vehicle redesign is expected to reduce cast iron and steel use by about 42 million pounds while adding roughly 5.26 million pounds each of aluminum and plastics as substitutes, plus about 2,200 troy ounces more platinum and palladium for larger catalytic converters — a 9 percent (not 13.7 percent, as initially estimated) increase for nonpassenger automobiles under 6,000 pounds. Secondary effects on water quality, industrial water demand, stationary-source air pollution, solid waste (because plastics resist landfill decomposition), and community noise are all characterized as minor. NHTSA concluded manufacturers had not shown a fuel-economy penalty from EPA's tighter MY 1979 NOx (nitrogen oxide) standard (lowered from 3.1 to 2.3 grams per mile), but accepted an 8 percent measured penalty from EPA's revised road-load test procedure (roughly a 30 percent increase in road-load horsepower setting).

evidence.quote: The agency estimates that 102,500,000 gallons of gasoline will be saved annually by the 1979 nonpassenger automobile fleet, over 1976 levels.
The annual and lifetime savings in gasoline would be between 0.07 percent and 0.1 percent of total national consumption based on total national consumption per year of 10.2 billion gallons in 1975.
The combined fleet savings for both classes would be between 69.1 million gallons and 102.7 million gallons per year and 691 million gallons and 1027 million gallons for the lifetime of the fleet.
The net energy savings are equivalent in BTU's to between 18.13 million barrels of oil and 26.9 million barrels of oil.

evidence.quote: The agency estimates a savings of steel and cast iron of 42 million pounds in MY 1975 over current levels of consumption which is 0.018 percent of the total national consumption of steel and cast iron of 236.2 billion pounds in 1975.

An increase of 16,200 troy ounces over the base of 180,000 troy ounces represents an increase of 9 percent, and not 13.7 percent as stated.
The agency believes that the additional use of 5.26 million pounds of plastics is likely to result in a minor increase in the solid waste disposal problem, particularly with respect to recycling.
It is anticipated that reductions of engine size, resulting from this standard, will have an imperceptible effect on community noise levels.
The change in the EPA emissions standard that affects fuel economy is the lowering of the standard for NOx from 3.1 grams per mile (gpm) to 2.3 gpm.

the NHTSA has concluded that the manufacturers have failed to show that there will be any penalty due to the tighter emissions standard. However, they have shown an effect of 8 percent due to the revised testing procedures.

public_response.text: Sixteen commenters weighed in, dominated by manufacturers — American Motors, Chrysler, Ford, General Motors, and International Harvester — plus the UAW, several federal agencies (EPA, FEA, Interior, Labor, Agriculture, Forest Service, offices within DOT), the Society of the Plastics Industry, Consumers Union, and the University of Michigan; NHTSA specifically noted that 'no comments were received from consumer groups, or other public interest organizations' with substantive input. Virtually all manufacturers argued the proposed 18.7 mpg was too high, primarily because of expected fuel-economy penalties from the MY 1979 emission standard and test-procedure changes, with penalty estimates ranging from 3 percent (Ford, emissions only) to 10-15 percent (International Harvester); several urged separate, lower treatment for four-wheel-drive jeep-type vehicles, which led NHTSA to add the two-class option. Ford also challenged NHTSA's cost-benefit analysis, arguing compliance costs would be at least $100 per vehicle rather than NHTSA's $12 manufacturer / $24 retail estimate, and AMC argued its Jeep CJ vehicle was not an 'automobile' under Title V and opposed including captive imports as discriminatory toward non-importers.

summary_of_interest.claim: This is explicitly the first federal fuel-economy standard ever set for light trucks, vans, and jeep-type vehicles, issued under a brand-new statute (Title V of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act, enacted December 22, 1975), and NHTSA deliberately limited it to a single model year while contemplating standards for heavier trucks and later years in future rulemakings.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: section 502(b) of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act directs the Secretary of Transportation to prescribe automotive fuel economy standards for automobiles which are "not passenger automobiles" in model years which begin more than 30 months after the date of enactment of Title V.
summary_of_interest.why_notable: The document is establishing the initial regulatory framework for what would become the federal light-truck CAFE program, and it defers key coverage questions (heavier trucks, later years) rather than treating them as settled.

evidence.quote: section 502(b) of the Motor Vehicle Information and Cost Savings Act directs the Secretary of Transportation to prescribe automotive fuel economy standards for automobiles which are "not passenger automobiles" in model years which begin more than 30 months after the date of enactment of Title V.

summary_of_interest.claim: NHTSA and every regulated manufacturer disagreed sharply over whether tighter 1979 NOx limits and revised EPA test procedures would impose a fuel-economy penalty, with industry estimates ranging from 3 percent (Ford) to 10-15 percent (International Harvester); NHTSA rejected the NOx penalty claims but accepted an 8 percent penalty from the road-load test procedure, cutting the proposed standard from 18.7 to 17.2 mpg.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: Every manufacturer challenged the assumption that the revised EPA emissions standard and testing procedures would have no effect on average fuel economy.
summary_of_interest.why_notable: The 1.5 mpg reduction in the final standard is a direct product of a technical dispute between NHTSA, EPA, and manufacturers, and reveals inter-agency friction over how EPA's own test-procedure changes should count against a DOT standard.

evidence.quote: Every manufacturer challenged the assumption that the revised EPA emissions standard and testing procedures would have no effect on average fuel economy.

summary_of_interest.claim: NHTSA created a separate, lower 15.8 mpg standard specifically for jeep-type four-wheel-drive vehicles (wheelbase not more than 110 inches) and gave manufacturers the option of counting those vehicles in either class — a subclassification added between the draft and final EIS in response to manufacturer comments, chiefly from AMC.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: The most significant changes to the draft EIS are the inclusion of the possible effects on fuel economy of the MY 1979 emission standard and the provision for two classes of NPA's. These changes result from comments made by the domestic manufacturers on both the NPRM and the draft EIS.
summary_of_interest.why_notable: Manufacturer comments — not public or environmental comments — restructured the rule from a single-class standard into a two-class scheme with manufacturer election, materially reducing stringency for jeep-type vehicles.

summary_of_interest.claim: NHTSA acknowledged on the record that no consumer or public-interest organizations submitted substantive comments on a first-of-kind national fuel-economy rule; the comment file was dominated almost entirely by the five affected manufacturers.
summary_of_interest.evidence_quote: Most of the comments were submitted by automobile manufacturers. There were no comments received from consumer groups, or other public interest organizations.
summary_of_interest.why_notable: For an environmental rule projected to save up to 1 billion gallons of gasoline, the total absence of consumer or environmental advocacy input left industry as effectively the sole outside voice shaping the final standard.
